source_title: India’s Industrial Power Must Go Beyond Borrowed Technology - Frontline Magazine
source_excerpt: India’s industrial strength should match tech autonomy center Reliance’s refinery complex at Jamnagar in Gujarat. India can choose which crude to buy. But its freedom is less complete when it comes to the technologies used to process it. By special arrangement By special arrangement https://fl-i.thgim.com/public/incoming/lsozdl/article71631216.ece/alternates/FREE_1200/Jamnagar%20refinery.jpg By special arrangement Dependence on imported components, proprietary processes and concentrated global supply chains exposes the limits of a growth model that prioritises production capacity over domestic innovation. INDUSTRY AND TECHNOLOGY India can bask in Marco Rubio’s praise for its capacity to refine Venezuelan oil, but it must use its industrial heft to encourage domestic innovation and promote the commercial deployment of home-grown technologies and processes. In the early 2000s, Indian governments used to showcase Bengaluru’s technology parks to foreign investors by branding the city as the next Silicon Valley. A decade later, India was the pharmacy hub of the world. On October 20, 2026, US Secretary of State Marco Rubio gave it another label: “India is a refining superpower.” He was in Mumbai, set to visit Reliance Industries’ Jamnagar refinery the following day. https://frontline.thehindu.com/the-nation/public-health/india-regulatory-data-protection-pharma-drug-prices-generics/article71359300.ece These labels mark genuine achievement, but leave something out. India has become indispensable to global production in software, medicines, and refined fuels. Yet, critical inputs, proprietary processes, and intellectual property remain concentrated elsewhere. The challenge is to convert manufacturing strength into ownership of the technologies that underpin it. https://frontline.thehindu.com/interviews/india-industrialisation-ha-joon-chang-interview/article70321699.ece Jamnagar’s importance to Washington lies not simply in its scale but in what its refining capabilities make possible. Reliance’s complex, with a combined capacity of approximately 1.4 million barrels per day, can process heavy and high-sulphur crude that many refineries cannot handle as efficiently. Rubio said he would encourage Reliance to refine more Venezuelan oil, giving the visit a significance beyond India’s industrial recognition. Washington’s search for buyers for Venezuelan supplies highlights a strategic asymmetry: the US is looking to Indian refining capacity to absorb additional oil, while India must decide how to use that industrial leverage without allowing its energy choices to become an instrument of US priorities. https://frontline.thehindu.com/the-nation/battleground-barsu-ecology-versus-economy-conflict-continues-over-refinery-project-in-maharashtra/article66838198.ece The US domestic context is important. The American Automobile Association reported a record national average diesel price of $6.53 per gallon on September 22. With US midterm elections approaching on November 3, fuel prices had become a politically consequential issue. The Russian oil question complicates this picture. In September, US President Donald Trump signed legislation authorising tariffs up to 100 per cent against major buyers of Russian oil and gas under specified conditions. On October 16, before the measures took effect, he waived their application without repealing the underlying law. The decision removed an immediate obstacle to negotiations with India, even as the US continued encouraging India to diversify its energy purchases. India should use its commercial options, buying Venezuelan, US, or Russian crude according to price, availability, and the applicable law. Being useful to Washington does not automatically translate into bargaining power. Reliance’s commercial interests and India’s energy-security priorities overlap, but they are not identical. Operating is not owning India can choose which crude to buy. But its freedom is less complete when it comes to the technologies used to process it. Reliance’s original Jamnagar refinery was built in the late 1990s with extensive foreign equipment, technology, and services, supported by a US Export-Import Bank loan guarantee. Modern refineries depend on specialised engineering, catalysts, process designs, and proprietary equipment supplied by a relatively small group of international technology companies. The question is how much of the technology deployed in Indian refineries is developed domestically and how much must be sourced from abroad. IndianOil’s INDMAX process is a revealing example. Developed by its research centre to upgrade heavy refinery residues into higher-value products, the technology was demonstrated at Guwahati in 2003 and has been deployed commercially at the Paradip refinery, Odisha, since 2015. In 2019, Serbia’s national oil company selected it through a global tender. IndianOil retains the underlying innovation, while US-based Lummus Technology serves as its global licensing partner and supplies proprietary hardware and design components. This is a commercialisation partnership, not foreign ownership. Yet it illustrates the distinction between developing a process and possessing every capability needed to commercialise it internationally. China’s Sinopec is a useful comparison. By its 2021 account, approximately 40 units had been designed using hydrocracking technology developed by its research institutes. China did not stop importing technology; it developed the capacity to absorb it, improve it, and sell its own. India needs the same progression from technological acquisition to adaptation, original research, and commercialisation. center A worker at a natural gas appraisal well of Sinopec in Langzhong county, Sichuan province, on March 1, 2011. Reuters Reuters https://fl-i.thgim.com/public/incoming/7cxupd/article71630979.ece/alternates/FREE_1200/worker%20at%20Sinopec%20Sichuan.JPG Reliance on imported technology and critical components raises questions about economic sovereignty, public investment and corporate power. The pharmaceutical and solar industries reveal related, though different, vulnerabilities. In 2024-25, China supplied 73.7 per cent of the $4.35 billion worth of bulk drugs and intermediates India imported. This dependence does not diminish India’s achievements in generic medicines, but it exposes the risks of relying on concentrated sources for critical inputs. In solar manufacturing, India’s approved-list module capacity reached 183 gigawatts by May 2026, yet NITI Aayog has highlighted continued dependence on imported polysilicon and wafers. Assembly capacity alone cannot secure an entire technological value chain. India’s gross expenditure on R&D stood at 0.84 per cent of GDP in 2023-24, according to the Department of Science and Technology. The 2013 Science, Technology and Innovation Policy described raising R&D expenditure to 2 per cent of GDP as a long-standing national goal achievable within five years. Public procurement can disadvantage new domestic technologies when tenders require an established commercial record that an unproven process cannot possess. Patient capital for the expensive transition from laboratory research to commercial deployment is also essential. ISRO, UPI, and India’s vaccine industry demonstrate that domestic institutions can develop technologies with international relevance. As Linsu Kim’s study of South Korea showed, late-industrialising economies can move from importing technology to assimilating it, improving it, and investing in original research. India has become adept at acquiring technology. The harder task is to turn domestic knowledge into commercially competitive products and processes. None of this argues against trade with the West. India should buy oil when the economics of it work, welcome investment, and pursue agreements that benefit its exporters. The question is what these relationships will contribute to domestic technological capabilities. Public-sector refinery expansions should create greater opportunities for proven Indian processes, as Paradip did with INDMAX. Procurement rules should allow credible domestic innovations to demonstrate their value rather than penalise them for lacking a commercial track record. A national mission on catalysts and process technology, bringing together IndianOil, Bharat Petroleum Corporation Ltd, Hindustan Petroleum Corporation Ltd, Engineers India, and private refiners, could pool expertise and support research through commercial deployment. A contribution linked to refining margins is one possible funding mechanism worth examining. Incentives for solar, batteries, and electrolysers should reward research and upstream manufacturing, not assembly alone. Foreign partnerships should be evaluated partly by the technical capabilities they build in India. Trade negotiations should also preserve the patent flexibilities that have helped sustain the generic pharmaceutical industry. For years, Bengaluru served as Silicon Valley’s back office, before it began to build for itself. The refinery of the world should also become its laboratory for R&D. India can welcome Rubio’s recognition of its industrial capabilities without confusing such recognition with technological autonomy. The real test is whether, a decade from now, the world is licensing Indian technology rather than merely praising Indian capacity. Tarun Agarwal is a Policy Research Fellow at the Indian Association of International Studies, New Delhi.
